lead: A classical error-correcting code adds redundant bits so a receiver can spot, and often repair, bits flipped by noise. Every real channel — a phone line, a Wi-Fi link, a QR code on a UPI sticker — corrupts some bits. The receiver computes a short check value, the syndrome, and matches it to an error pattern. This chapter builds repetition codes, Hamming distance, linear codes with matrices G and H, and works Hamming(7,4) end to end.
prereq: You need binary arithmetic and basic probability, plus the noisy-channel picture from 5.5.

blocks.text: The simplest code repeats each message bit. In a 3-bit repetition code, 1 becomes 111 and 0 becomes 000. Three channel bits carry one message bit, so the rate is 1/3. The receiver takes a majority vote: the value appearing at least twice wins, so one flipped bit is outvoted.

The Hamming distance d(x, y) between two binary strings is the number of positions where they differ. For example d(101, 111) = 1 and d(101, 000) = 2. The weight of a string is its distance from all zeros, that is, its number of 1s.
A code C is a set of codewords. Its minimum distance d_min is the smallest Hamming distance between any two different codewords. The repetition code {000, 111} has d_min = 3.

blocks.where: t is the number of bit errors the code always corrects; d_min is the minimum distance between codewords; ⌊·⌋ is the floor (round down). d_min = 3 corrects t = 1; d_min = 7 corrects t = 3.

blocks.text: The same distance sets detection. A code with minimum distance d_min detects up to d_min − 1 errors, because the received word then cannot land on another codeword. Correction is harder: the decoder must also decide which codeword was meant. The bound t = ⌊(d_min − 1)/2⌋ comes from geometry: spheres of radius t around codewords must not overlap.

sections.h3: Linear codes, G and H, and the syndrome

blocks.text: A linear code is a set of binary vectors closed under addition modulo 2 (XOR). Its size is 2^k, so each codeword carries k message bits. An (n, k) code turns k message bits into n channel bits, with rate R = k/n.

Two matrices describe the code. The generator matrix G is k × n; the codeword is c = mG, where m is the message row vector and all arithmetic is mod 2. The parity-check matrix H is (n − k) × n with G Hᵀ = 0. A vector r is a valid codeword exactly when H rᵀ = 0.

That last fact is the decoding tool. Suppose c is sent, an error pattern e flips some bits, and r = c + e arrives. Then H rᵀ = H cᵀ + H eᵀ = 0 + H eᵀ. The syndrome s = H rᵀ depends only on the error, never on the message, so the receiver looks up the most likely error from s and subtracts it: ĉ = r + ê.

items: Compute the syndrome s = H rᵀ, an (n − k)-bit column vector.
If s = 0, accept r as a codeword.
Otherwise, the column of H equal to s names the most likely single flipped bit.
Flip that bit, then read the message from the data positions — positions 3, 5, 6 and 7 in Section 3's layout.

blocks.text: For this lookup to work for every single error, the columns of H must be nonzero and all different. That is exactly how Hamming codes are built. A code that corrects t errors needs every sum of up to 2t error columns to be distinct — the same sphere-packing idea as before.

Hamming(7,4) takes k = 4 message bits and produces n = 7 channel bits, so the rate is 4/7. It has d_min = 3 and corrects t = 1 error. Three parity bits join four data bits. Write a codeword as (p₁ p₂ d₁ p₃ d₂ d₃ d₄).
p₁ = d₁ ⊕ d₂ ⊕ d₄,  p₂ = d₁ ⊕ d₃ ⊕ d₄,  p₃ = d₂ ⊕ d₃ ⊕ d₄
blocks.where: d₁…d₄ are the four message bits, p₁ p₂ p₃ are the parity bits, and ⊕ is addition mod 2 (XOR). Each parity bit covers a different subset of data bits.

blocks.text: Take the message 1011, so d₁ = 1, d₂ = 0, d₃ = 1, d₄ = 1. Then p₁ = 1⊕0⊕1 = 0, p₂ = 1⊕1⊕1 = 1, p₃ = 0⊕1⊕1 = 0. The codeword is 0 1 1 0 0 1 1, written 0110011.

For decoding, the three checks are s₁ = p₁⊕d₁⊕d₂⊕d₄, s₂ = p₂⊕d₁⊕d₃⊕d₄, s₃ = p₃⊕d₂⊕d₃⊕d₄. Read (s₃ s₂ s₁) as a binary number: 0 means no error, and 1 to 7 give the flipped position. That is why parity sits at positions 1, 2 and 4, the powers of two that act as bit labels. Suppose 0110011 is sent and 0110001 arrives, with bit 6 (d₃) flipped. The received bits are p₁=0, p₂=1, d₁=1, p₃=0, d₂=0, d₃=0, d₄=1. Then s₁ = 0⊕1⊕0⊕1 = 0, s₂ = 1⊕1⊕0⊕1 = 1, s₃ = 0⊕0⊕0⊕1 = 1. Reading (s₃ s₂ s₁) = 110 gives 6, so the decoder flips bit 6 back.

figure.caption: Each message bit is repeated three times. The first block arrives as 101 instead of 111, and majority vote still returns 1.

spec.title: Repetition code, rate 1/3
spec.aria: Each message bit is repeated three times; majority vote corrects the flipped bit in the first block.

examples.question: A 3-bit repetition code is used on a binary symmetric channel. The message 101 is encoded and 101 000 111 is received. (a) Decode by majority vote. (b) State how many errors the code corrects and detects. (c) Give the code rate. (d) If two bits in the first block flip, what does the decoder output?
steps: Encode: 1 0 1 gives blocks 111, 000, 111, so the transmitted word is 111 000 111.
Blocks 2 and 3 arrive as 000 and 111; the first block arrives as 101.
Block 1 has two 1s and one 0, so majority vote gives 1. Blocks 2 and 3 give 0 and 1. Decoded bits: 1, 0, 1.
Correctable errors t = ⌊(3 − 1)/2⌋ = 1. Detectable errors = d_min − 1 = 2.

Two flips in 111 leave one 1 and two 0s (100, 010 or 001). Majority vote returns the wrong bit, 0. The block is not a codeword, so the error could be flagged, but a plain majority-vote decoder outputs a silently wrong 0.
examples.answer: Decoded bits 1, 0, 1; corrects t = 1 error, detects 2 errors, rate 1/3 ≈ 0.333; a double flip in a block gives the wrong bit.
examples.check:
msg = [1, 0, 1]
blocks = [[b]*3 for b in msg]
received = [[1,0,1], [0,0,0], [1,1,1]]
decoded = [1 if sum(r) >= 2 else 0 for r in received]
print(''.join(map(str, decoded)))
d_min = 3
t = (d_min - 1) // 2
print(t)
print(d_min - 1)
print(round(1/3, 3))
double = [1,0,0]
print(1 if sum(double) >= 2 else 0)

code.code:
def encode(bit):
    return [bit, bit, bit]

def majority(block):
    return 1 if sum(block) >= 2 else 0

message = [1, 0, 1]
transmitted = [encode(b) for b in message]
received = [[1, 0, 1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 1, 1]]
decoded = [majority(b) for b in received]
print('encoded:', transmitted)
print('received:', received)
print('decoded:', decoded)

d_min = 3
t = (d_min - 1) // 2
print('d_min =', d_min)
print('corrects t =', t)
print('detects =', d_min - 1)
print('rate = %.3f' % (1/3))
print('two flips ->', majority([1, 0, 0]))

examples.output:
encoded: [[1, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 1, 1]]
received: [[1, 0, 1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 1, 1]]
decoded: [1, 0, 1]
d_min = 3
corrects t = 1
detects = 2
rate = 0.333
two flips -> 0

traps: A distance-3 code corrects one error, not two. Two flips in a block beat majority vote and give a silently wrong bit.
Detection and correction differ: d_min detects d_min − 1 errors but corrects only ⌊(d_min − 1)/2⌋.
The syndrome depends only on the error pattern, not on the message sent.
All matrix arithmetic in binary codes is mod 2: 1 + 1 = 0.
Rate is k/n, message bits over transmitted bits — not over parity bits.

quiz.q: State the formula for the number of errors a code with minimum distance d_min can correct.
Why does the syndrome H rᵀ not reveal the message?
quiz.a: H cᵀ = 0 for every codeword c, so H rᵀ = H eᵀ depends only on the error e, not on which codeword was sent.

quiz.q: A code has codewords {0000, 1110, 1001, 0111}. Find d_min and the number of errors it corrects.
quiz.a: Distances: d(0000,1110)=3, d(0000,1001)=2, d(0000,0111)=3, d(1110,1001)=3, d(1110,0111)=2, d(1001,0111)=3. Smallest is 2, so d_min = 2 and t = ⌊1/2⌋ = 0: it detects one error but corrects none.

quiz.q: For Hamming(7,4) with p₁ = d₁⊕d₂⊕d₄, p₂ = d₁⊕d₃⊕d₄, p₃ = d₂⊕d₃⊕d₄, encode 1011.
quiz.a: d₁=1, d₂=0, d₃=1, d₄=1. p₁ = 0, p₂ = 1, p₃ = 0. Codeword (p₁p₂d₁p₃d₂d₃d₄) = 0110011, rate 4/7 ≈ 0.571.

quiz.q: In a 3-bit repetition code, the first block of 111 is hit by two errors. Explain the decoder's output and why this is a failure of the code, not the decoder.
quiz.a: Two flips turn 111 into a word with two 0s, e.g. 100. Majority vote gives 0, the wrong bit. With d_min = 3 the error spheres have radius 1, so a two-error word sits closer to another codeword. The code is not designed for two errors.

quiz.q: Why must the columns of H for a single-error-correcting code be nonzero and pairwise distinct?
quiz.a: A single flip in position i gives syndrome s equal to column i of H. A zero column would make that error invisible. Two equal columns would give the same syndrome for two different errors, so the decoder could not tell which bit to fix. Distinct nonzero columns correct all n single errors.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real systems stack these ideas: QR codes use Reed-Solomon codes and survive a scratched payment sticker, 5G uses LDPC codes, and hard disks use BCH codes. Classical codes also scaffold quantum error correction, where the stabiliser formalism plays the role of the parity-check matrix — see 5.7. Worth searching next: Reed-Solomon, LDPC, BCH, and the Hamming bound.
